title: Bicerin Torinese
author: Marco Bellini
desc: Turin's celebrated layered drink of espresso, thick drinking chocolate, and whipped cream, served in a small glass so the distinct layers remain visible, historically enjoyed unstirred.
longDesc: Bicerin has been a fixture of Turin's historic cafés since the 18th century, and tradition holds that it should be sipped slowly through its layers rather than stirred together, allowing each element — bitter coffee, rich chocolate, cool cream — to be tasted somewhat distinctly.
ingredients: 80 g (2.8 oz) dark chocolate, finely chopped
80 ml (⅓ cup) heavy cream, whipped to soft peaks
steps: Warm the milk gently in a small saucepan, then add the chopped chocolate and sugar, stirring until fully melted and smooth.
Continue heating gently, stirring, until the mixture thickens slightly into a rich, drinkable chocolate.
Pour the hot chocolate mixture into the bottom of small clear glasses.
Gently pour the hot espresso over the back of a spoon on top of the chocolate layer, to keep the layers distinct.
Top with a generous dollop of softly whipped cream, again pouring gently to preserve the layers.
Serve immediately, traditionally enjoyed without stirring.
chefTips: Pouring each layer gently over the back of a spoon helps keep the distinct layers from mixing together.
The chocolate layer should be thick and rich, more like a drinking chocolate than thin cocoa.
Traditionally sipped slowly through its layers rather than stirred, allowing each element to be tasted somewhat separately.
commonMistakes: Pouring the layers too forcefully, causing them to mix together rather than staying distinct.
Making the chocolate layer too thin, losing the rich, velvety quality that defines a proper bicerin.
Stirring immediately, which is contrary to the traditional way of enjoying this layered drink.
servedWith: Enjoyed on its own as an after-dinner treat or afternoon pick-me-up
storage: Not applicable; made and consumed immediately.
healthBenefits: Best enjoyed as an occasional indulgent treat given its rich chocolate and cream content.
culturalNote: Bicerin has been served in Turin's historic cafés since the 18th century, and remains one of the city's most iconic culinary traditions, inseparable from its coffeehouse culture.
